title: Peter walks on water (Matthew 14:22–33)
hookLine: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and is caught by the hand
tomorrow: Who do you say I am?

lines: THE MOMENT BEFORE YOU STEP OUT.
THE FOURTH WATCH OF THE NIGHT.
A FIGURE WALKING ON THE SEA.
cards: The first day of a new job. Asking someone out. Standing up to speak.
There's a moment where you step out or don't. Back to the lake, the same night as the boy's lunch. Jesus sends the disciples ahead in the boat and goes up a mountain alone to pray.

Out on the water the wind is against them, and the waves toss the boat. Then, Matthew says, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see him coming toward them, walking on the sea. They scream.

teach.h: BE OF GOOD CHEER; IT IS I.
teach.b: Straightaway he speaks, in the King James Bible: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid."
And Peter, of course it's Peter, answers: "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water." One word comes back: come. Peter climbs over the side, and actually walks.

teach.h: HE SAW THE WIND, AND SANK.
teach.b: Then: "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me." That's the whole shape of it.
He steps out, looks at the wind instead of the one he's walking toward, and sinks. A three-word prayer, no time for more.
Then: "And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" Immediately. The hand comes first, the question after.
Little faith, in Matthew's Greek, is one word, oligopistos, almost a nickname; Matthew's Jesus uses it for his disciples more than once.
Little faith, not no faith: enough to step out, not quite enough to keep looking up.
When they climb back in, the wind stops, and the people in the boat worship him and say, of a truth thou art the Son of God.
So end two weeks on the road through Galilee: stargazers, a family fleeing, a boy asking questions, a wild man, a river, a desert, full nets, a party, a wedding, a well, a lunch, a storm.
And now a man sinking, and a hand.

how: Many Christians pray Peter's words, Lord, save me, in moments of fear, and the story is often preached on trust and doubt. Icons and paintings of the scene show Christ's hand reaching for Peter as he sinks.

o: of no faith at all, an unbeliever
of great faith, bold enough to step out
of little faith, though not of none

games.q: you're Peter. you've stepped out of the boat and you're walking on the water. then you feel the wind and start to sink. what do you do?
o: swim back to the boat on your own.
games.why: he cries out, Lord, save me, and immediately Jesus stretches out his hand and catches him.

practice: Think of one step you've been waiting to feel ready for, a call, an application, an apology, a hard conversation, a first try, and picture just the first step over the side.
Notice where your eyes go, to the wind, to what could go wrong, then remember the hand in the story, which came immediately. If you pray, you can use Peter's three words.

wordCard.voice: Oligopistos. One Greek word for you of little faith, Jesus's nickname for Peter after he stepped out and began to sink. These two weeks' words: the magi, the Holy Innocents, baptism, disciple, semeion, the Samaritan woman, the storm.

orig.note: Greek: you of little faith. One word, almost a nickname, that Jesus uses for his disciples more than once in Matthew.

carryVoice: Your line: he catches the sinking. Tomorrow the road turns toward Jerusalem, with a question. Week eight, complete.
